subject: english-literature

moments.title: Dickens writes A Christmas Carol
moments.who: Charles Dickens, struggling to support a growing family
moments.body: Dickens writes the Carol in six weeks (October-November 1843), partly walking the London streets at night to think it through. Self-published with Chapman & Hall in December, with John Leech's illustrations. 6,000 copies sold by Christmas Eve.
moments.takeaway: Dickens micromanaged the book's production. He earned less than expected because of his choice to use expensive production and a low price. He revised that approach for later books.

moments.title: Dickens reads the Carol
moments.body: Dickens performed public readings of the Carol from 1853 onwards. His American tour (1867-68) included 75 readings; his earnings — and his exhaustion — were enormous. The performance tradition shapes how the story is read aloud at Christmas.
moments.takeaway: Dickens essentially invented the modern celebrity author tour. The Carol was his most-performed work.

moments.title: Dickens dies
moments.body: 9 June 1870: Dickens dies suddenly at 58, leaving Edwin Drood unfinished. The Times: 'England has lost her greatest novelist.' He is buried in Westminster Abbey against his wishes (he wanted Rochester).
moments.takeaway: Dickens at his death was probably the most famous Englishman in the world, ahead of Gladstone or Tennyson. His readership crossed every class.

now.title: The author of Christmas
now.body: Dickens's A Christmas Carol substantially invented the modern English Christmas — family, charity, redemption, generous feeling. The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992), Scrooged (1988), countless stage versions and adaptations keep it in continuous circulation. Modern phrases ('Bah, humbug,' 'Tiny Tim') derive entirely from it.
now.open_questions: How sentimental is too sentimental? Modern readers sometimes find the Carol cloying; Victorian readers, less moved by every Christmas film of the past fifty years, took it as a serious moral text. The cultural reception shifts.

reflection: A six-week novella in 1843 created the Anglo-American Christmas as we know it. Dickens's combination of social criticism, sentimental redemption and indelible characters makes the Carol one of the most efficient pieces of cultural engineering in English literature.
